lessons.title: Certified phones
lessons.why: A bargain SIP phone is not a Teams client. The certified list is the product boundary.
body: Teams-certified phones sign in as Teams users and use the Teams media stack. SIP Gateway covers a smaller set of compatible SIP and analog devices, with a smaller feature list. Check the current list before you buy.
QoS for phones follows the same DSCP story, with device-specific notes in the rooms and devices articles. A phone that never registers is often identity or Conditional Access, not a codec.
lessons.say: I buy from the current certified list, or I use SIP Gateway for the devices it actually supports.
lessons.fault: A generic SIP phone is forced into the design and never registers.
lessons.listen: Use Teams-certified phones or the SIP Gateway device list. Do not invent a third category.

lessons.title: Teams Rooms
lessons.why: A room account with a user license and a strict Conditional Access policy is a dark screen at the start of a meeting.
body: Rooms use the current Teams Rooms license. Do not borrow a user Calling Plan and hope. The room resource account must be allowed to sign in as a device. Conditional Access that assumes an interactive user will lock it out.
QoS for Teams Rooms is documented separately for Windows and Android. Include the room in the same DSCP plan as the PCs, and test a call from the room, not only from a laptop.
lessons.say: Rooms get a room license and a Conditional Access exception you can explain.
lessons.fault: The room has a user E5 stack and still cannot sign in.
lessons.listen: License Teams Rooms with the current room SKU and let the device sign in.

lessons.title: SIP Gateway and analog
lessons.why: Elevators, door phones, and fax machines do not run the Teams client.
body: Leave analog on a certified SBC or on SIP Gateway when the device is supported. Direct Routing is the usual way to keep those devices when the humans move to Teams. A Calling Plan user license does not create an elevator phone.
Test the emergency path from the analog device, including during a WAN cut if the device must keep working. An elevator that depends on a cloud sign-in is a bad surprise.
lessons.say: Analog stays on the SBC or SIP Gateway, with an emergency test from that device.
lessons.fault: The elevator is migrated to a Teams user and fails when the WAN fails.
lessons.listen: Keep analog devices on an SBC or SIP Gateway, and test their emergency path.

lessons.title: Media bypass
lessons.why: Bypass changes where RTP flows. It does not change where SIP flows.
depends: a client that can reach it
body: With media bypass enabled on the gateway, media can run directly between the Teams client and the SBC instead of through Microsoft’s media processors. Signaling still uses the PSTN hubs. Microsoft does not support re-targeting that media mid-call.

Bypass is a candidate when the user is on a network that can reach the SBC. A full-tunnel VPN is a poor candidate. Location-based routing may forbid the path. AMR-WB is listed for non-bypass only. If bypass is off, open UDP 3478–3481 and 49152–53247.

flow.label: Media
flow.detail: Client to SBC, SIP still to Teams

lessons.say: Bypass is media only. SIP still goes through Teams. I check LBR and the VPN first.
lessons.fault: Bypass is enabled for VPN users and audio gets worse.
lessons.listen: Media bypass skips the media processor, not the SIP proxy. Turn it on only when the client can reach the SBC.

lessons.title: Local media optimization
lessons.why: A branch SBC with one public interface can still hairpin local users out and back.
body: Local media optimization uses internal and external SBC interfaces so a user inside the branch stays on the local media path. It is more specific than a single bypass checkbox. Use the current article and the SBC vendor’s build.
If internal users hairpin to the public address of an SBC sitting on their own LAN, you have not finished the design. Draw the interfaces before you enable the feature.
lessons.say: Local media optimization is about which SBC interface the media uses. I will draw both.
lessons.fault: Users on the LAN hairpin through the public internet to reach an SBC in the same rack.
lessons.listen: Local media optimization keeps branch media on the internal SBC interface. Draw the interfaces.

lessons.title: Common area phones, again, as devices
lessons.why: The license sentence and the device sentence meet at the hallway.
body: A common-area phone is a device account plus a number plus a policy. On Direct Routing it does not need a Calling Plan. It still needs a supported phone and a network path that can reach Teams.
Do not reuse a departed employee’s number by signing the phone in as that employee. That is how caller ID and voicemail become someone else’s mailbox.

flow.label: License
flow.detail: Fits Direct Routing or Calling Plan

lessons.say: A common-area phone has its own account. I will not sign it in as a person who left.
lessons.fault: The hallway phone deposits voicemail into a former employee’s mailbox.
lessons.listen: Give common-area phones their own accounts and the license that matches the connectivity option.
